q63v93.text: Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week. Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored. OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said. The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said. The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it. The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack. The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls. One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server. On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections. "A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer. The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found. The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys. One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt. A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab. A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint. Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt. In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned. The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties. The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week. Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted. What the Providers Have Disclosed An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections. Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated. A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window. At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts. Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers. Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three. The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week. What Users Should Do The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price. Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check. Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys. A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

1dwe0eu.text: A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it. Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly. Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks. Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses. The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files. The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering. Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor. WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index. Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory. WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other. Updating the Renderer The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced. Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system: Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix. Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell. One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point. The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

guedox.text: Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC. Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient's organization was affected that same day. "On 17 November 2026 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC), an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot," reads the notification. According to Rackspace, the attackers were able to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations, allowing them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys that can be used to access databases, cloud services, and other systems. Rackspace warned that the attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user's clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user. The company says it has since revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring. Affected customers have been instructed to reissue their Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets. Rackspace also advised customers to analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials. The company shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the attack: IP address: 23.224.79.106 IP range: 23.224.0.0/15 Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe BleepingComputer contacted Rackspace to ask how many customers were affected and whether customer data was stolen, but has not received a response. The breach also caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console, temporarily preventing customers from managing their clusters and rotating potentially compromised credentials. In a Reddit discussion, Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of Platform9, which co-developed Rackspace Spot with Rackspace, explained that the company deliberately disabled access while securing its infrastructure. "I've been instrumental in creating Spot and in its operations to date, and I can tell you that the team and I are incredibly disappointed to have let you down in this way," Raghuram said. "I know you disagree, but we made the decision that shutting all access down and sanitizing the entire environment is what we can do to best protect everyone using Spot." After multiple delays, Rackspace announced that service had been fully restored on November 21. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 161mlqr.text: Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information. Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center. According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit, Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23. An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations. "On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification. The company says the exposed information included: Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts. Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information. Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp. Connect Health onboarding status. An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024. Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API. However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information. Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations. Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post. Some managed service providers (MSPs) also reported receiving notifications for multiple customer tenants, with one administrator saying the emails arrived hours apart. The notification says no software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability. However, Microsoft recommends that organizations alert their security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks that could target the exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information. Organizations are also advised to ensure privileged accounts use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, review their Connect Health configurations, and examine Microsoft Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft also published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts that allows administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed. However, the script displays current configuration values rather than the information that was accessed during the breach. Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began. When contacted by BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that it had fixed the vulnerability and notified impacted customers. "We identified and addressed a security issue affecting Microsoft Entra Connect Health that could have resulted in unauthorized access to tenant-level contact and configuration metadata. We deployed a fix on November 19, 2026, and have notified impacted customers through Azure Service Health, providing guidance and support," a Microsoft spokesperson told BleepingComputer. Microsoft declined to provide further details about the breach. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1azlhxy.text: The BADBOX malware botnet has returned following last year's disruptions, generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests per day through infected Android-based devices. According to HUMAN's Satori researchers, who uncovered and disrupted the latest variant, BADBOX 3.0 had grown into the largest documented ad-fraud operation by daily bid request volume. BADBOX was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon. In December 2024, Germany's cybersecurity agencies warned that the botnet had infected tens of thousands of devices. In March 2025, a large-scale disruption operation took place where HUMAN and Shadowserver cut off more than 500,000 BADBOX 2.0 devices from their control servers, while Google removed 24 apps that spread the malware from Google Play. Google later sued the botnet's operators, saying the BADBOX 2.0 had infected over 10 million Android-based devices by April 2025. BadBox returns However, the previous disruptions didn't stop the BADBOX operators from rebuilding the botnet and setting new records for daily fraudulent advertising bid requests. "At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform," reports HUMAN. "BADBOX 3.0's volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years' worth of published Satori investigations combined." Bid requests volume Source: HUMAN The modus operandi remains the same: infecting cheap phones, tablets, and streaming TV boxes running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) with malware that performs ad fraud and traffic proxying. The malware performs ad fraud by playing video ads in hidden windows while impersonating legitimate streaming apps to make the requests appear legitimate. HUMAN also observed fraudulent server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests that tricked advertisers into believing ads were played on streaming devices, even though no actual device or video ad was involved. A proxying module also enrolled infected devices in one of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners' knowledge or consent. One of those networks, PXYEDGE, was identified as the rebranded successor to IpMoYu, a residential proxy service previously linked to BADBOX 2.0. The researchers say PXYEDGE advertised approximately 200,000 proxy nodes, while their monitoring showed unique connections peaking at around 340,000. HUMAN says some of the ad fraud traffic was also routed through these residential proxies to appear legitimate and evade anti-abuse filters. BADBOX operational overview Source: HUMAN The researchers linked the malware to a specific Chinese electronics manufacturer through its domains, device-specific checks in the code, a factory-installed TV launcher, and a repository maintainer. The infected devices fetch malware modules from public code repositories, while the same payloads are also mirrored across various hosting platforms for redundancy and to resist takedowns. HUMAN says it also participated in Google's disruption of the related XCPE malware operation earlier this month, which included taking down multiple C2 domains used by BADBOX 3.0. Additionally, one of the malware repositories was taken down, while HUMAN says its systems now filter fraudulent advertising traffic associated with BADBOX 3.0. However, HUMAN warns that the botnet operators are likely to adapt to the latest disruption, as they have done in the past. Users should only buy certified Android devices from reputable manufacturers and ensure that Play Protect is available and active. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1u90zlh.text: FBI systems have reportedly been breached for the second time in two months, this time targeting the agency's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which is used to share information between local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. The National Crime Information Center is an FBI-operated database used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share information about wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, protection orders, and other criminal justice records. Police officers routinely use the system during traffic stops, criminal investigations, and background checks. According to CNN's reporting, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the NCIC system, citing two people briefed on the investigation. The intrusion was reportedly discovered in recent days, although it is unclear when the breach occurred, how the attackers gained access, or whether any information was stolen. The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident and did not respond to CNN's request for comment. The reported breach comes just two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have breached the FBI's systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability. The earlier attack targeted a third-party platform associated with the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, with ShinyHunters claiming to have stolen sensitive information from the agency's systems. The FBI subsequently launched an investigation that led to the arrests of suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attacks. There is currently no indication that the latest NCIC incident is connected to ShinyHunters or the earlier breach. It remains unclear whether the attackers accessed sensitive law enforcement records stored in NCIC or whether the intrusion affected the system's availability to law enforcement agencies. BleepingComputer contacted the FBI on Friday evening with questions about the reported breach but has not received a response. pivlb6.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Artificial Intelligence A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown. The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts. The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer. There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach. Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage." In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up. From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown. That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent. The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines. Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through. The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in. The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

1dc8sa6.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program. Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages. The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out. Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says. The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG. When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details. The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier. What to Update The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. What to install depends on where the library sits: Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory. Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible. Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch. Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases. GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed. The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

aqj2tu.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cyber Espionage Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week. The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled. The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install. MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework. The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder. The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected. Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history. Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report. The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company. Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it. A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root. That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do. In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise. The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot. Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install. The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw. What to Do Now With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach: Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs. Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default. Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to. Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched. If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used. The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described. The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

10d76gs.text: Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete." The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen. It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature. Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." "The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy." The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk. Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android). "However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said. "Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system." Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data. Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users - Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup. On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications. In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post. "We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said. "In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents." Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings. Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

19fccy5.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 21, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026) CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025) CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026) Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884. The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor. The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

1jcu2n2.text: West Virginia’s state legislature is responding to a cyberattack that has taken down its website and impacted IT systems. Ann Ali, deputy chief of staff for the House of Delegates, told Recorded Future News that the attack started on Thursday and has continued through Friday. “Upon discovery, the relevant teams immediately took steps to contain the incident and began an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity specialists,” Ali said. “In connection with the investigation, access to certain Legislature IT systems has been temporarily disabled. However, based on what we know so far, the incident appears to be limited to the Legislature’s computer systems.” She added that no other state agencies or offices are impacted by the cyberattack. An investigation into the incident is ongoing but Ali did not respond to follow-up questions about whether it was a ransomware attack. No hacking groups have taken credit as of Friday. The West Virginia legislature is split between two bodies, a Senate and a House of Delegates with 134 total members representing the state’s 1.7 million residents. Multiple municipalities in the state have dealt with ransomware attacks in recent years, including the cities of Beckley and Westmoreland. Security research firm Comparitech tracked 132 ransomware attacks on government bodies across the U.S. in the third quarter — a 91% increase compared to Q3 last year. At least 41 of the attacks involved U.S. based municipalities, including a major incident impacting Anne Arundel County in Maryland. This week alone, residents of South Portland, Maine, lost access to critical city services due to a cyberattack, while Minnesota’s Otter Tail County notified its 61,000 residents of a data breach caused by a ransomware attack in July.

1c3t0nw.text: A new congressional report focused on how some American companies are embedding China-developed open weight artificial intelligence models into their tech stacks calls the trend alarming and cautions U.S. firms against the practice. Pointing to how Huawei and ZTE technology quickly found their place in the marketplace and threatened American networks, the new report warns that if China-developed open-weight models are allowed to take root, removing them down the road will take several years and cost taxpayers billions. Open weight models’ numerical weights and biases are made public for download. The joint investigative report — produced by the House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party — focuses on Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor coding platform owner Anysphere as examples of companies deploying Chinese open weight models. The companies were using them for customer assistance, coding projects and taking inventory. None of the firms immediately responded to a request for comment. Report co-authors Reps. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) and John Moolenaar (R-NY) drew the 50-page-long report’s findings from hearings, classified briefings, and agency advisories. The lawmakers also received briefings from DoorDash, Airbnb and Anysphere about how they integrated China-developed open-weight models into their consumer platforms, enterprise software and other systems. “The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay,” the report said. “While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.” Silicon Valley startups and Fortune 500 companies alike are adopting Chinese open-weight models because they are cheap, easily customized and work well, according to the report. But those benefits come with significant negatives, the report said, citing federal investigators’ findings showing that Chinese developers “used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities.” The report features 12 policy recommendations, including the imperative to build an American open-weight AI initiative, establish a standard for where models are sourced from, create an AI bill of materials, bar China-developed models from federal contract work and sensitive critical infrastructure functions and evaluate Chinese models systematically. The report is important because it identifies and explains the risks posed by the U.S. not competing seriously in the low cost open-source model marketplace, according to Mark Montgomery, a cybersecurity expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. Because China is more limited in the frontier model space — dominated by U.S. firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI — its leaders have pursued a strategy to expand global dependence on their open-source AI, using the “traditional Chinese model of state policy and capital” to kill competition, he said. “Companies and utilities, driven by bottom line resource decisions will, as always, ignore security and safety issues in pursuit of a lower front end cost,” he said. “China knows this recipe well.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

udok25.text: The Container Store on Friday said it is recovering from a cyberattack that forced it to shut down its online ordering systems and limited in-store transaction processing. The firm’s parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, said in a statement that The Container Store has “restored its website and systems following a cybersecurity incident this past weekend.” Neighborhood Intelligence — a rebrand of Bed Bath & Beyond — purchased The Container Store in July for $150 million. While the stores remained open throughout the week, they had to use “alternative transaction-processing procedures,” according to the statement. The Texas-founded company has about 100 stores across the U.S. Neighborhood Intelligence said the incident only impacted The Container Store and did not affect its other brands including Bed Bath & Beyond, Overstock, buybuy BABY or Kirkland’s. Neighborhood Intelligence reported $509 million in revenue for the third quarter earlier this month, with the increases driven primarily by the acquisition of The Container Store. The company said it hired cybersecurity experts to contain the incident and restore the affected systems. So far, it does not appear the hackers stole customer financial data, but did not address claims made by the cybercriminal group n0n, which listed the company on its leak site earlier this month. The n0n cybercriminal group emerged in September, and cybersecurity experts say they specialize in ransomware and data extortion. The group has attacked more than 100 victim organizations and demanded hundreds of millions of dollars in ransoms. The group initially forced victims to pay a 10% fee just to access its negotiation portal, but now forces companies to pay the full ransom before viewing any sample of the stolen information, according to SOCradar. Allan Liska, a ransomware expert at Recorded Future, said the group launched its data leak site in late September and tried to recruit affiliates on a Russian cybercrime forum called RehubcomPro Forum in late October. Liska said the group’s cybercriminal post claimed affiliates were instructed to only target companies that earn more than $10 million annually in revenue and were banned from attacking organizations in the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Record is an independent unit of Recorded Future. Cybersecurity firm LevelBlue said the group has primarily targeted healthcare and pharmaceuticals but recently claimed to have troves of data from financial services companies and retail firms. LevelBlue noted that the group has used an AI coding agent and paid AI services to write and debug its attack scripts, helping it scale operations quickly. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1xgbk0i.text: Bell Canada has confirmed that an "agentic" threat actor breached its systems on November 17, 2026, and stole enterprise customer data, including information from a system used to order and provision telecommunications circuits. Bell is one of Canada's largest telecommunications providers, offering wireless, internet, television, and enterprise networking services. BleepingComputer first learned of the incident after receiving a tip from a customer who shared a breach notification sent by Bell's Information Security Team. According to the notification, an unauthorized party accessed a pre-production environment of Bell's Maximo system, which the company uses to order and provision telecommunications network connections. Bell warned that information belonging to the recipient's organization may have been stolen, including business contact information such as names, job titles, corporate email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. The potentially exposed data also includes information contained in ticket titles and some IP addresses associated with network elements or systems, along with limited contextual information. However, Bell said the affected dataset did not contain credentials, highly sensitive personal information, PDFs, file attachments, or other supplementary information stored in Maximo. When contacted by BleepingComputer, Bell confirmed the intrusion and said that an "agentic threat actor" had accessed multiple systems and stolen enterprise customer data. "Bell is investigating a cybersecurity incident that occurred on November 17 in which an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data," Bell told BleepingComputer. "Upon learning of the breach, we immediately contained the incident and secured our systems. There has been no impact to customer services." The company's description of the attacker as "agentic" suggests that AI-powered tools were used during the breach. Bell says it is sharing indicators of compromise (IOCs) and threat-hunting information with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS). However, Bell has not publicly released the indicators of compromise and has not responded to BleepingComputer's request to share them so other organizations can check their environments for related activity. Bell told BleepingComputer that it has not yet identified the threat actor responsible for the attack. "We currently do not know the attribution," Bell said. Bell has not disclosed how many enterprise customers were impacted or the total amount of data stolen. In its customer notification, Bell urged organizations to remain cautious of unsolicited requests and social engineering attempts by individuals impersonating the telecommunications provider. 1ghlyk1.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4. The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said. The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue. When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful. Also addressed by the company are two other flaws - CVE-2026-102769 - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted. CVE-2026-44908 - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70. Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message. It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. "Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation." WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

1u8jd9l.text: Hackers used an autonomous AI agent platform called "Cairn" to discover a zero-day vulnerability in a medical imaging application and exploit it to take complete control of a server. According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, the suspected Chinese-linked attackers simply instructed the AI agents to "obtain shell access," leaving them to independently discover and exploit the flaw. Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the campaign after discovering that the attackers had left their Cairn instance publicly accessible without authentication, exposing their hacking operations. According to the researchers, the attacks were launched by a Chinese-nexus threat actor between September 8 and 10, 2026, targeting mainly East Asian educational institutions outside China. Cairn is a legitimate pentesting tool that can be used to coordinate multiple AI agents in cyber-operations, created for research and defense strengthening. Gambit Security documented cases of Cairn abuse as part of a large-scale credit card stealing operation in September. More recently, Google reported it was deployed in an attack against an aerospace organization in the U.S. During the campaign investigated by Amazon, the AI agents were not always successful. For example, a 16-hour and 148-action effort to take control of a Redis server failed. In a separate case targeting a university GPU server, the agents tried over 30,000 credential combinations over six hours but failed to brute-force their way in. Finding and using a zero-day According to Amazon, Cairn's AI agents found a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging application that uses AI to help researchers label medical images. The flaw enabled the agents to write files to arbitrary locations on the server, and within 11 minutes, they went from mapping the application's API to exploiting the vulnerability. In a subsequent session, the AI agents used the flaw to write a Python reverse shell to the sitecustomize.py file that automatically loads when Python starts, then triggered an API endpoint to establish root access to the server. After discovering the zero-day, the operator provided the agents with a proxy into a second university network running the same vulnerable software and directed them to target other machines. Amazon reported the flaw to MONAI Label maintainers, and they released a security update to address it on November 18. The researchers attributed the campaign to a Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language of the retrieved prompts, the activity timestamps, and the choice of targets. Amazon also shared two IP addresses associated with the campaign, observed between September 8 and 10, 2026: 142[.]4.98.145 142[.]4.107.34 Amazon warned that AI agents can find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than security teams can react, urging organizations to rely more on automated defenses rather than manual investigations.
