1n5cj2j.text: Chinese hackers used an AI tool called Cairn to allegedly discover a zero-day while breaching several universities in Asia, according to a new report from Amazon’s Threat Intelligence team. CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said their investigation began on September 10, when they discovered a publicly accessible server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn — an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework. They were able to view the operational history of the platform, including previous prompts and more. The operator wrote their prompts in Simplified Chinese and the timestamps were configured to China Standard Time. The targeted victim organizations were universities in East Asia. Moses explained that Cairn is ideal for attackers because, when given a starting point and objective in plain language, it can coordinate multiple AI agents to complete a task. In this incident, the attacker provided IP addresses and asked Cairn to “obtain shell access” — meaning find a way to gain enough access to a system for various actions to be taken. “Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step,” Moses said. One of the attempts involved 148 actions taken over 16 hours that were ultimately unsuccessful, including a failed attempt at exploiting the Log4Shell vulnerability. Another failed effort saw Cairn try for more than six hours to breach university servers by testing more than 30,000 credential combinations tied to 80 real usernames. The only successful attempt occurred when the agents discovered a vulnerability in an open-source medical imaging AI application and exploited it. “At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched,” Moses said. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.” The attacker then used the same apparent zero-day to breach a second university. Moses said Amazon Threat Intelligence contacted the maintainers behind the open-source medical imaging AI application and they fixed the bug that was discovered. He added that AWS “worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.” AWS declined to name the universities or the country they are in. Moses said the campaign stood out because of the speed and operational tempo of the AI agents. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes “completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert,” Moses warned, noting that the agents “ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints.” Artex vs. Cairn Cybersecurity researchers and law enforcement agencies have released multiple warnings in recent weeks about AI-backed offensive cyber tools that are being used by attackers, particularly those from China. The FBI published an advisory about AI tool Artex one week ago, writing that it could take any large language model and turn it into a powerful hacking tool that can “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.” Artex was implicated in multiple attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions while Microsoft said Artex was used by Chinese state-backed actors in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise. Moses said last week that Artex was seen used in credential theft attacks on AI models and in campaigns targeting crypto exchanges. Cairn was also spotlighted by Google researchers on Tuesday in a report about the evolving use of autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI and others. Google noted that it saw Cairn used in intrusions of companies in the U.S. aerospace sector and wrote, like AWS found, that it was adept at starting with a target’s IP address and ending with an operational objective. The AWS report on Cairn cites a study released in September by cybersecurity firm Gambit Security that documented the use of Cairn by a financially motivated hacking group using the tool to breach online retailers. Eyal Sela, Director of Threat Intelligence at Gambit Security and the researcher behind the report, told Recorded Future News that Cairn is more significant than Artex because it is a general-purpose tool. “While it is good at solving ‘red team’ or capture-the-flag tasks, it can also solve other problems and the main point is that it has no internal structuring for cybersecurity,” Sela said. “When a tool is more generic, it is less predictable because it has less structuring around the way it solves a task.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

fb56hx.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale. Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan. "Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping." One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background. Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API. One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities - Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store. One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed - A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager A downloader that directly downloads the main payload It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them. "Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]." The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically. "Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging." "When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon." Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely. Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels - Control, which is used to issue commands Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft - call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones contacts, to collect contact information device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands file_manager, to access the file system input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy push, to create and manage local Android notifications screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards toast, to display text messages on the device's screen twofa, to capture one-time verification codes uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian. "ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application." "Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest." ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data. "What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said. Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers. Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure. An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features - Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device Abuse accessibility services for full remote control Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password "The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said. "To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off." Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations. "By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

pvhm8w.text: The National Security Agency has mostly returned to business as usual after patches to a commonly-used programming language caused an internal communications network to crash for much of the week. The spy agency is operating under “normal conditions, with exceptions” today, according to a Friday morning voicemail inbox recording for its workforce. Certain facilities remain under “Code Orange” for non-essential employees, meaning delayed openings and some must check in with their supervisors. The instructions come after three days of disruptions to NSANet, which allows employees to communicate classified information internally. The disruptions were attributed to maintenance affecting PHP, a ubiquitous programming language. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in a television interview earlier this week. Workplace interruptions also occurred at NSA Georgia. Intelligence operations at that facility, focused on the Middle East, were not negatively impacted, according to two sources familiar with the situation. The outages also did not curtail NSA’s ability to support President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, where he met with the leaders of China and Russia, these people said. Administration officials have insisted the problems at the spy agency are not the result of a cyberattack and not connected to other IT woes that have impacted Microsoft products, airline travel and online banking services in recent days. NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

ru51sd.text: J.P. Morgan Chase warned it suffered a data breach after a cyberattack at a third-party service provider exposed customers' personal information and marketing data. The bank said the incident didn't disrupt its services and is unrelated to a service disruption that occurred earlier this week. "We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack," reads the firm's announcement on X. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses." J.P. Morgan Chase Bank is the largest U.S. bank by assets, with about $4.1 trillion as of June 2026. Its consumer banking division reports about 78 million active digital customers. Visa and Mastercard separately confirmed third-party incidents in statements to the media, though they have not confirmed any impact on customers. The two firms are major global payment network operators with presence in more than 200 countries, handling annual transaction volumes of multiple trillion USD. "Visa is aware of these claims. They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," a Visa spokesperson told BleepingComputer. "Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week." Mastercard told BleepingComputer that they "were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program." Mastercard's spokesperson assured that "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards." "At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed." n0n ransomware claims the attack On November 11, 2026, the n0n ransomware group claimed responsibility for an attack on Qubole, suspected to be the third-party provider the payment services use. 1m67ezi.text: The password spreadsheet your admins use may look like a complete inventory, but it only reflects some of the credentials employees have reported using. More specifically, that spreadsheet doesn’t show passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the document was last updated, until someone brings it up to date. That’s assuming someone ever does. Meanwhile, work passwords can end up in all kinds of places. Someone saves one in their browser. A teammate sends a shared login in chat to move forward with a project. Another employee decides to put a few passwords in a personal vault because getting access to the company one takes too long. Unless someone reports these actions, the spreadsheet won’t capture them. And so, admins may think they have a handle on company credentials when, in fact, their spreadsheet tells only part of the story. The real reason credentials slip out of admins’ view The predominant factor is convenience. When the approved process is slow or unclear, employees use what’s at hand: a browser’s built-in password storage, a shared Google document, a Slack message, or one of the sticky notes on their desk. They may know that that’s against the rules, but in the moment, their priority is getting work done. That’s why a process that relies on employees to manually report every new password, update, and shared credential is nearly impossible to sustain. If the official route feels like an obstacle rather than the easiest way to access work tools, people are more likely to work around it. This preference for convenience shows up in people’s password habits, too. Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found that, in the median case, only 49% of users’ passwords across different services were unique. In other words, more than half of those passwords were reused. The “TOP 20 Not-So-Secret Business Passwords” report by NordPass has also found “123456” to be the world’s most common password used in a corporate setting. This shows that people generally take the easy route when it comes to passwords. Without visibility, a company may not even know that one of its most important assets is protected by “123456” or another weak password. To solve this problem, organizations need an approach that works for both employees and admins. Without one, credentials can remain scattered and difficult to manage, increasing the risk created by those blind spots. The risks of poor visibility into company credentials When admins can’t see where work credentials are stored, they also cannot know who uses them, who they’ve been shared with, or whether they’ve changed. They also cannot assess the strength and reuse of the passwords employees rely on every day. Verizon’s report found that only 3% of compromised passwords in its dataset met basic complexity standards. That finding doesn’t describe every password in an organization, but it shows why teams need a way to identify weak credentials in the systems they manage. Reuse matters, too: if a password is compromised, reusing it across services can put more than one account at risk. This leads us to the most important element, which is that credentials still remain one of the main ways attackers gain unauthorized access to company systems and data. The 2026 edition of the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified credential abuse as the initial access vector in 13% of breaches. It also found that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31% of breaches, underscoring the need for credential protection as part of a broader security strategy. Keeping company credentials in a spreadsheet creates another risk. If ransomware attackers gain a foothold in the company network, they may search specifically for files containing passwords. Ransomware groups such as Pysa have used automated scripts to scan drives for filenames and folders containing terms like “password,” “login,” “pwd,” and “passwd.” If attackers find a spreadsheet, they may encrypt it and demand a ransom. They could also use the credentials inside to access other accounts and systems, potentially spreading the attack further. The solution? A structured approach that’s easy for admins to manage and for employees to follow. To keep company accounts protected, admins should be able to answer a few questions about each company password: Is it strong? Who owns it? Where is it stored? Who has access to it? Is it reused, old, or exposed in a breach? Each factor matters because any one of them can create risk. A strong password could still be reused across multiple accounts, so if it’s exposed in a breach, attackers may be able to use it to access those other accounts, too. A recent password change won’t tell you whether the right people still have access, either. Reviewing factors like these helps admins understand what needs attention. But how can they keep track of all of it? The right password manager can make this easier by giving your team one place to store and manage work credentials. NordPass, for example, offers organizations a centralized vault protected by XChaCha20 encryption and a zero-knowledge architecture, which means the service provider can’t access what’s stored inside. NordPass also helps admins check the credentials in the vault. With features like the Data Breach Scanner and Password Health, it can quickly identify weak, reused, old, and exposed passwords. With NordPass, admins can also set password requirements to make sure all credentials used by employees are strong, while users can share credentials securely over protected channels. Beyond that, the Sharing Hub feature shows who has access to passwords shared with multiple people or teams, and the activity log records actions related to company passwords. All of this gives admins a way to spot credential issues early, decide what to address first, and check what changed afterward to make sure company logins are as secure as they can be. What a managed vault won’t solve on its own A password manager can help solve the visibility problem, but it won’t address every aspect of it. Some employees may continue saving passwords in browsers or personal vaults, so adoption depends on making the approved option easy to use and setting clear expectations about how company logins should be handled. Shared accounts may need clearer ownership, too. Your IT team should decide who is responsible for each login, who needs access, and when that access should be removed. It’s also important to bear in mind that not every credential is a password. API keys, recovery codes, certificates, and other secrets may need their own storage, access, and ownership rules. Therefore, a password health report shouldn’t be treated as a complete inventory of every way employees access company resources. Stronger credential security starts beyond the spreadsheet A password spreadsheet or any other manually updated document can’t provide a reliable view of your company credentials. But a secure business password manager like NordPass can. It gives your team a secure place to store work credentials, shows you how healthy the passwords in the vault are, and makes it easier to set password requirements, share credentials securely, and track password-related activity. So, if you really want to know what’s happening with your company credentials, give NordPass a try, and replace the spreadsheet with a business password manager built for the job. 10mzvul.text: N-able says attackers who breached one of its servers have caused a major outage affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services worldwide. On Tuesday, the company initially blamed the outage on what it described as a "combination of platform configuration and service dependencies" affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts services across the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and Europe. However, one day later, N-able disabled UI and API access and confirmed unauthorized access to a server in the Hosted Cloud environment. N-able also said the cyberattack didn't affect email flow or spam filtering and that it has yet to find evidence that the attackers gained access to customers' data and mailboxes. "Our earlier update said the disruption came from platform configuration and service dependencies and we believed we had remediated the issue. As we continued our investigation, we determined that the disruption was caused by a security incident affecting the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment," the company said. "We are aware of unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud. We have taken steps to mitigate the threat and are continuing to harden our services to reduce the risk of recurrence. The investigation is ongoing, but at this time we do not have evidence that customer data was compromised, including access to tenants' mailboxes." After detecting the attack, N-able also alerted customers via email and took down the management portal (dashboard), as well as quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization supporting services. "Until these services are restored, customers may be unable to sign in to the control panel, view or release quarantined messages, review logs, or make configuration changes such as adding or removing domains," it added. N-able says this is unrelated to an N-central incident that forced it to take all hosted N-central environments offline to patch more than 30 zero-day flaws affecting its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform. As BleepingComputer previously reported, hackers are now also exploiting a newly disclosed N-able zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable N-central servers. 1rwvmxm.text: A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean. On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled. Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off. Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2. In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday. The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change. Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it. Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD. There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt. Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud. Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU. Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed. Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it. The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT. The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years. In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities. What to Do The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted. Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range. Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected. Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change. Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it: Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on. If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration. Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again. The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

91ebfq.text: Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027. The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters. The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it. Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence. Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents. In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system. Mapped onto security operations, the four stages look like this. Evidence collection. Querying the SIEM and EDR, pulling process trees, enriching indicators, gathering identity and cloud context. Analysis and verdict. Correlating what was collected, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether the alert is a real threat. Response recommendation. Proposing what should happen next, such as containing a host, resetting credentials or closing the case. Response execution. Actually changing something in the environment. This split gives security leaders a cleaner set of choices. A team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system. Human IN the loop vs. Human ON the loop Once autonomy is split by stage, teams need a shared way to describe how much of it each stage gets. A useful vocabulary comes from researchers at the University of Washington, who define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays. Level Human role What it means in practice L1 Operator The human directs and decides, and the agent carries out instructions L2 Collaborator Human and agent plan and execute together L3 Consultant The agent leads and checks in for expertise or preferences L4 Approver The agent works independently and asks for approval only in risky or predefined cases L5 Observer The agent acts on its own while the human monitors and can hit the stop button The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart. Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is. A highly capable agent can still run at L2 if the stakes call for it. Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic. Enterprises evaluating AI SOC vendors should make sure that both models can be applied as appropriate, across their entire operations. How to decide where and how much autonomy to grant an AI SOC The levels mentioned above tell you what the options are. Deciding where each SOC action belongs takes a rubric, and three questions do most of the work. Reversibility. If the agent gets this wrong, how quickly and completely can it be undone? Blast radius. How many users, systems or business processes does the action touch? Receipts. How strong and verifiable is the evidence behind the decision? An action backed by forensic proof of what was executed deserves more latitude than one backed by an LLM hunch about what looks suspicious. Scoring real actions against those questions produces a map that most security teams will recognize. Example action Reversibility Blast radius Suggested starting level Query SIEM, EDR or identity logs Nothing to reverse None L5, fully autonomous Enrich indicators and pull process trees Nothing to reverse None L5, fully autonomous Close a false positive with a full evidence trail Easy, the case can be reopened Low L4, autonomous with sampling review Open and route a ticket to an owner Easy Low L4, autonomous with sampling review Block a known malicious hash or domain Easy Low to medium L4, autonomous within defined policy Isolate a standard employee laptop Moderate One user L3 or L4, approval for sensitive groups Disable an account or revoke sessions Moderate One user, possibly many if a service account L3, approval required Isolate a production server or domain controller Hard Business-wide L2, human decides and agent executes The exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point. The rubric forces an explicit decision for each action, instead of a single policy that is either too loose for the dangerous actions or too tight for the safe ones. When human approval becomes a rubber stamp According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. It sounds like the safe choice, and in many cases it is. It also hides a failure mode that rarely gets discussed. Human approval is only as good as the context the reviewer receives. When an approval step arrives without clear evidence or criteria, reviewers start clicking through requests to keep the queue moving, and oversight quietly disappears. If the AI shapes how every investigation is framed, the human approving the final action is approving a conclusion they never saw being reached. Only when the reviewer can actually check the AI’s logic and work along with hard, forensic evidence that conclusively points in one direction or another, is the approval actually worth anything. In practice that means every approval request should show three things. The evidence the agent collected and where it came from. The reasoning that connects that evidence to the verdict. What the agent checked and ruled out along the way. A useful test if this is working, is time spent. If a reviewer cannot verify a verdict in a minute or two, the approval step is ceremonial and the team is paying for a human-in-the-loop without getting it. Autonomy you earn, autonomy you lose The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications gives this approach a name. It extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks and letting that autonomy grow as it is earned. Earning it requires criteria that are set before the pilot starts. Otherwise autonomy expands on vendor promises and gut feel. A practical set of graduation criteria for moving an action class up one level looks like this. Measured agreement. Track how often the agent's verdicts match analyst review over a defined period and alert volume, and set the threshold in advance. Dry runs first. Run new actions in a test mode that executes the logic but mocks every write, so the team sees what the agent would have done before it does anything. A complete evidence trail. Every decision at the new level must be auditable after the fact, including what the agent looked at and why it concluded what it did. A rollback path. Define how the action is undone and who owns that before expanding scope. Autonomy should also move down. A drop in agreement rates, a major change in the environment such as a new EDR or cloud migration, or a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. Teams that only ever ratchet upward are building risk they cannot see. Your SOC agent is an agent too Every level of autonomy granted to a SOC agent has a second effect. It raises the damage that agent can do if it is wrong, manipulated or compromised. Security leaders already feel this risk across the enterprise. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions. The lesson for the SOC is that autonomy itself is a risk factor, scored alongside the vulnerability. Treat the AI SOC agent the way you would treat a new privileged identity. Give it its own identity, never shared credentials. Scope its permissions to the actions it is approved for at its current level. Log every tool call, query and action in a form a human can review. Watch it with the same detections you would apply to a new admin account. A playbook for the next 12 months The move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. Security leaders who want the capacity gains without the incident that sets their AI program back a year can start with five steps. Inventory every action. List everything your AI SOC agent can do today, from read-only queries to response actions, and place each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric. Automate investigation aggressively. Evidence gathering and analysis consume most analyst hours and carry the least risk. This is where full autonomy pays off first. Gate disruptive response with real evidence. Keep approval on high-impact actions, and make sure every approval request carries proof a reviewer can verify quickly. Write graduation and demotion criteria now. Agree on the accuracy thresholds, test periods and rollback paths before the pilot starts, so autonomy expands on data. Govern the agent like a privileged identity. Scope it, log it and monitor it, because its autonomy is also its blast radius. Crossing the trust threshold Every SOC that adopts AI agents will eventually face the same question for each action. Is the agent's work trustworthy enough to act on without a human checking it first? A helpful way to think about it is a trust threshold. Below it, AI assists analysts, and humans still validate every conclusion. Above it, teams can safely hand off execution and supervise outcomes instead of steps. What moves an action across that line is depth and proof. An agent that can show what actually executed, where it came from and what it did, gives a human something real to verify, and gives the organization a defensible reason to extend its autonomy. Forensic-level investigation, the approach Intezer’s AI SOC is built on, is what moves an action across that line. That is what earned autonomy means in practice. The agent gets more authority one action class at a time, each step backed by evidence the team can inspect, and each step reversible if the evidence stops holding up. Note: This article has been written and contributed by Zev Schonberg, PMM at Intezer.

o3gbhx.text: US cybersecurity company F5 warned customers to patch five BIG-IP vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to trigger denial-of-service (DoS) or gain remote code execution. Tracked as CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-116953, and CVE-2026-123637, these stack-based buffer overflow flaws affect the company's BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) centralized access management proxy solution and the BIG-IP iRules programmable scripting feature. All five security issues are rated critical severity, and unauthenticated threat actors can exploit them to terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute arbitrary code remotely on systems with vulnerable configurations. The company also released engineering hotfixes for a high-severity BIG-IP APM SAML vulnerability (CVE-2026-126822) stemming from an integer underflow (wrap or wraparound) weakness that remote, unauthenticated threat actors can abuse in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. "Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system and may perform RCE," F5 said. "There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only." F5 said it has no mitigation measures for these flaws and advised security teams to install the out-of-band hotfixes released on Wednesday to address them on vulnerable devices. Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver currently tracks more than 177,000 BIG-IP instances and over 14,600 IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints exposed online. However, there is no information on how many are honeypots or have already been patched against these vulnerabilities. Internet-exposed BIG-IP instances (Shadowserver) Although the company hasn't flagged any of these issues as exploited in attacks, admins should upgrade systems to the latest version as soon as possible, since cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often abused F5 vulnerabilities in the wild. Attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive files from victims worldwide in recent years. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged seven F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited since November 2021, four of them also used by ransomware gangs. Most recently, in September, F5 also patched a critical BIG-IP APM vulnerability (CVE-2026-94127) that is being actively exploited in zero-day remote code execution attacks. One year ago, F5 also disclosed that state-backed hackers breached its systems in August 2025 to steal source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities. F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to more than 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 of Fortune 50 companies. wo5w0u.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Network Security / Vulnerability SonicWall has urged all customers still running Generation 6 firewalls to retire and replace them immediately and stop exposing the devices on the internet edge, citing security risks fueled by AI-assisted attacks. "Attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever," SonicWall said. "We expect internet-facing Gen 6 firewalls to be actively targeted. Treat any Gen 6 firewall still in service as a high-risk exposure, and migrate to a supported Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8." The affected products running SonicOS 6.x include - TZ350, TZ350W, TZ500, TZ500W, SOHO 250, SOHO 250W NSA 4600, NSA 5600, NSA 6600 NSa 4650, NSa 5650, NSa 6650 TZ400, TZ400W, TZ600, TZ600P, NSA 3600 NSa 3650 NSa 2650 SOHO, SOHO W, TZ300P, NSa 9250, NSa 9450, NSa 9650 NSv 10 to NSv 1600 (Gen 6 virtual) SuperMassive 9200, 9400, 9600, 9800 NSsp 12800, NSsp 12400 TZ300, TZ300W NSA 2600 In recent years, threat actors have increasingly targeted edge devices as a launch point to obtain initial access, even as the window between disclosure and confirmed exploitation has collapsed significantly, in part driven by threat actors' use of automation and AI to scan the internet for unsupported devices, analyze patches and vulnerability disclosure announcements, and build working exploits faster. According to Google Mandiant's M-Trends report published in March 2026, the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities has turned negative, reaching an estimated -7 days, meaning exploitation, on average, begins before a patch is available, down from 63 days in 2018 and -1 day in 2024. "This trend is compounded by threat actors' evolving interest in security appliances and networking infrastructure," Google said. "Because these assets provide critical inspection of data ingress and egress points, they grant significant visibility and permissions to those who gain access to them." Cisco Talos' 2025 Year in Review report has also found that 23% of CVEs discovered in the year directly impact network devices like VPN appliances, next-generation firewalls (NGFWs), load balancers, routers, and others. "Since these systems sit at the perimeter of enterprise environments, compromise may lead to direct access to the critical networks," Talos said. "This aligns with real-world trends from CISA'sKnown Exploitation Vulnerability (KEV) catalog, where exploitation consistently favors edge devices because they are internetfacing, often lag in patching, and provide direct operational leverage once compromised." With Gen 6 no longer being actively supported and receiving patches, even for critical flaws, users are recommended to follow the steps below without any delay - Inventory every Gen 6 firewall in the production environment and retire them. Prioritize units that are exposed to the internet or provide remote access. Replace them with a Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8 Contact an authorized SonicWall partner to plan the migration Until the firewall is replaced, it's advised to take the below actions to minimize exposure - Disable WAN management (HTTPS, SSH, and SNMP on WAN interfaces). Disable SSL VPN, or restrict it to known source addresses. Enforce multi-factor authentication on every remaining remote-access and admin account, and reset local passwords. Disable services and interfaces not in use. Monitor logs closely for unusual logins, configuration changes and traffic. "The risk to an unsupported firewall grows every day it stays online," SonicWall said. "One breach reaches everything. A compromised perimeter firewall gives attackers a foothold for credential theft, lateral movement and ransomware deployment."

ykgdri.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit. The activity involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root. "This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies," Cisco said in an advisory released late last month. "Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated." "An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device." Patches for the flaw were released in the following versions on October 21, 2026 - Cisco Expressway Series Release X14 and earlier - Migrate to a fixed release Cisco Expressway Series Release X15.5.3 and earlier - X15.5.20 In a report published Thursday, Russian cybersecurity company F6 said it observed what appears to be the first case of in-the-wild exploitation of the flaw to gain remote command execution on compromised Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices with root privileges after a PoC exploit became publicly available. "The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices," F6 said. "Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization's internal network." Following root access, the attackers are said to have undertaken efforts to move laterally across the network and use custom Python scripts to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive data. Analysis of the scripts indicates that they were possibly developed with assistance from artificial intelligence (AI) tools, given the presence of comments and descriptions of fixes. The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the activity - IP addresses geolocated: 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116 Presence of "wombat@127.0.0.1" in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices Python scripts staged in "/mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py" The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Users are advised to update to the latest supported version of Cisco Expressway, audit environments for signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, determine the scope of the attack, and block potential lateral movement vectors. "This incident demonstrates that compromise of a perimeter device can open a path for an attacker to an organization's critical systems," F6 said. "That means protection should therefore include not only timely vulnerability remediation but also properly configured segmentation and infrastructure monitoring."

yf0n2c.text: The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions - VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200 VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract) VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2) "CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said. "Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local." An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW. "BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said. The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW. From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment. "The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW." Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities - SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance. BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server. SAWSNAKE, a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, thereby making it possible to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tokens, bypass multi-factor authentication(MFA), and impersonate any user. It's a Go-based port of an open-source Python script named "vcenter_saml_login.py." BEARBONES, a C backdoor based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server that's capable of bypassing system password authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from the temporary directory. LAZYBONES, a lightweight Go backdoor that uses Slack for command-and-control (C2) communications and has been previously deployed in a separate intrusion in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of a critical flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2025-22457, CVSS score: 9.0). It's suspected that Armory Castle had knowledge of the flaw prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026, with the recovered BONESAW binary containing a build timestamp of July 13, 2026. However, it's worth noting that build metadata can be modified before compilation. "After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, Armory Castle moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-<REDACTED>@vsphere.local," Google said. "Notably, Armory Castle enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. After enabling SSH, Armory Castle connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account." In the final stage of the attack, the adversary was found enumerating the ESXi file system, mounting Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and adding an SSH public key to the root account's authorized keys. It also conducted additional reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi file system, which were then archived and downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance for subsequent exfiltration. Furthermore, the attackers have been observed dropping LAZYBONES to a separate Linux appliance, which periodically checks for commands from a designated Slack channel, allowing it to perform command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. CVE-2026-123890 is the second vulnerability in a VMware product to be exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day this year alone. Late last month, CrowdStrike revealed it identified incidents where the hacking crew abused CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging flaw in VMware ESX, to reduce audit trail visibility. "BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days," Google said. "The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each." "The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting Armory Castle operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor's operational commitment to compromise high-priority targets."

gno2yr.text: Microsoft released the KB5132057 November optional cumulative update for Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 26H2, which comes with 28 changes, including improvements to Windows Search, Windows Hello, and the Run dialog. KB5132057 is a preview update that allows IT administrators to test Windows improvements, bug fixes, and new features before they become generally available in next month's Patch Tuesday release. However, unlike regular Windows cumulative updates, monthly optional updates don't include security fixes and provide only quality improvements. The KB5132057 update includes the new Windows Search Box experience that was built on WinUI 3 and removes promotional content from web results for better resource efficiency and a streamlined design. After installing the November 2026 preview update, users will also get improved Windows Hello facial recognition that lets them sign into their accounts in dark rooms after enabling the "Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition" option under Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello). KB5132057 also adds the new Run dialog, unveiled in May with a refreshed design and an almost instant time-to-show of just 94 ms. After installing the update, you can enable it by toggling on "New Run dialog" under Settings > System > Advanced. You can install KB5132057 by opening Windows Settings, clicking on Windows Update, and then clicking 'Check for Updates.' KB5132057 preview update (BleepingComputer) ​Since KB5132057 is an optional update, click the "Download and install" link if you don't already have the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" option enabled, which would prompt the OS to install it automatically. You can also manually download and install this preview update from the Microsoft Update Catalog. Windows 11 KB5132057 highlights Once installed, this optional non-security update will upgrade Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2 devices to builds 26300.10075 and 26200.10075, respectively. The November 2026 preview update comes with many other changes, some of the most significant ones highlighted below: Search from This PC in File Explorer is now indexer-based, making it much faster and consistent with search from File Explorer Home. Inline actions: You can now complete common tasks directly from Windows Search without opening Settings. For example, you can turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange open windows. If you have an Android phone connected through Phone Link, you can also call or text contacts and use phone actions like “Find my phone” and “Do Not Disturb.” New! If you accidentally trigger the keyboard shortcut for Sticky Keys, Filter Keys, or Toggle Keys, you can now turn it off directly from the prompt that appears. You can still manage notifications and sounds for these features under Settings > Accessibility > Keyboard > Notification preferences. New! Web sign-in is now supported on Microsoft Entra hybrid-joined devices, in addition to Microsoft Entra-joined devices. At the lock screen, you can sign in without a password by using a FIDO2 security key, a passkey on your phone, or a Temporary Access Pass (TAP). After you sign in, Windows gets a Kerberos ticket, so access to on-premises file shares and internal sites continues to work. For more information, see Web sign-in for Windows. [File History] This update fixes an issue where the File History restore interface might not find backups when a drive is selected as the backup location. On Thursday, Microsoft also warned customers that their devices may reboot one more time after deploying the November 2026 optional update and updates rolling out over the next months. "With recent and upcoming Windows updates over the next few months, a limited number of consumer and business devices might experience one additional restart during installation," Microsoft noted in a message center update. "This one‑time restart occurs after a Secure Boot certificate update is applied as part of the Secure Boot update process." Microsoft announced this will be the final non-security preview update released this year, as operations wind down for the Western holidays. Normal monthly servicing will resume in January.
