7nygyq.text: E-commerce platform Cleverbridge is warning that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers and CVV security codes. Cleverbridge provides e-commerce services to software and SaaS companies, allowing them to sell products, process payments, and manage subscriptions. The company lists numerous technology brands as its customers, including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony, and Parallels. However, it has not disclosed which businesses' customers were impacted by the breach. In a new page about the security incident, Cleverbridge says it detected unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026, and temporarily took systems offline to contain the breach. "All systems were brought back online on 4 November 2026; however, our investigation subsequently determined that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform," reads the security incident disclosure. Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, warning that hackers had stolen payment card details used to make purchases through its platform. While its public disclosure confirms the theft of payment card data, it does not specify which card details were stolen, instead referring affected customers to their individual notifications for more information. However, a breach notification shared with BleepingComputer reveals that the stolen information includes payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC security codes. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes the payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC)," reads the notification. "Note however that no other personal data (for example your name, contact or billing details) were copied. The affected card ends in XXXX." BleepingComputer redacted the last four digits of the affected payment card. The company has not disclosed how the attackers gained access to its platform, how long they remained in its systems, or how many customers were affected by the breach. Of particular concern is the theft of CVV/CVC security codes, which are used to verify payment card transactions. Cleverbridge also confirmed that the incident was not a ransomware attack and that attackers did not encrypt any of its systems. The company says it has notified data protection authorities, law enforcement, payment card networks, and payment partners about the incident. Cleverbridge is also working with TransUnion's Cyberscout to distribute breach notifications and provide affected customers with complimentary credit monitoring and fraud assistance. Affected customers are told to review their payment card statements for unauthorized transactions. Cleverbridge also recommends contacting card issuers about the incident, as banks may decide to replace compromised cards. BleepingComputer contacted Cleverbridge with questions about how many customers were affected, how the attackers accessed its systems, whether the stolen payment card data was encrypted, and why CVV/CVC security codes were accessible. y44w7c.text: Signal has announced new protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and prevent AI assistants from capturing conversations on supported Android devices. The protections are designed to stop Siri and Gemini, the AI assistants built into iOS and Android, from accessing private conversations while performing tasks for users. The change comes after Signal introduced a feature in May 2025 that blocks Microsoft's controversial Recall screenshot-capturing feature on Windows 11. "We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen," Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post. Whittaker says OS-level features such as Siri's Onscreen Awareness and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture chat content as it appears on the app's screen, putting potentially sensitive private data outside Signal's control and exposing all conversation participants. Option to block Siri scanning on Signal for iOS Source: Signal Signal says its engineers spent months figuring out how AI systems access app data, designing targeted protections to block all extraction pathways verified through reverse engineering. However, Signal warns that AI agents could still access conversations through other methods, which Whittaker describes as "an existential threat to Signal." She explains that AI agents could access conversation data in multiple ways, as they are now embedded deep in operating systems, leaving apps vulnerable and with limited options for protecting users. The most notable example is macOS, where Signal says it's currently unable to provide any screenshot-blocking protection. For macOS 27 users, Signal recommends adding the app to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri to prevent Siri AI from proactively accessing message content. For this reason, Signal calls on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to fully disclose, through detailed documentation, all potential access mechanisms and give app developers a clear way to opt out of AI access across screens, files, notifications, and APIs. Signal did not provide specific app version numbers for the new protections but says they are automatically activated when possible. Signal recommends that users upgrade to the latest available version and go to Settings > App Security to check that Block Siri AI is enabled on iOS. On Android, Signal says it automatically enables Screen Security when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. However, on iOS, the protection also prevents users from taking screenshots of their Signal conversations, even for legitimate purposes. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss.
